caption:
Flood season in the Niger-Benue system is a dam-management problem before it is a rainfall problem. Nigeria's worst flood years correlate with controlled dam releases upstream, not just local precipitation. When reservoirs approach capacity, operators release water to protect the structure. That release becomes a downstream surge with days of lead time before it hits a floodplain community.

The same lag applies to pipeline theft economics. Tapping a line is low-cost and low-skill relative to the resale value of diverted product. As long as that spread holds, enforcement that relies on ground patrols alone will keep losing the arithmetic. The theft sites move faster than the patrols can.

Both problems share a structure: the actionable signal exists before the visible damage does. A release upstream, a new access track to a pipeline right-of-way — these show up in the collection window ahead of the flood crest or the spill. The gap is not information. It's who is watching the right window at the right time.

Pipeline theft runs on simple economics: low cost to tap, high resale value for diverted product. Ground patrols alone can't win that arithmetic — the tap sites move faster than the patrol schedule.
Both problems share a pattern: the actionable signal precedes the visible damage. An upstream release, a new access track near a right-of-way — both are observable before the crest or the spill.
The gap isn't a lack of information. It's coverage timing against a moving problem.

card.headline: The flood starts upstream
card.sub: Dam releases and pipeline economics both generate warning signal before the visible damage. Coverage timing is the gap, not information.

rationale: Grounds the brand in real regional dynamics using only public knowledge, reinforcing the collection-timing thesis without overreaching into unproven detection claims.
